notes.definition: A polymer is a substance made of very large molecules (long chains) in which atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds. The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
explanation: Polymers have very large molecules. Each molecule is a long chain made of many small repeating sections called repeat units joined together, often thousands of them. A familiar example is poly(ethene), the polymer used to make plastic bags and bottles. Within each polymer molecule, every atom is linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, for example the carbon to carbon bonds along the chain and the carbon to hydrogen bonds at the sides.

A polymer is still made of separate molecules. The chains are not covalently bonded to each other. Between neighbouring chains there are intermolecular forces. For small molecules such as methane or water these forces are weak, but the strength of intermolecular forces increases with the size of the molecules. Because polymer molecules are so large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong.

This is why polymers are solids at room temperature. To melt a polymer, the chains must be able to move past each other, so energy must be supplied to overcome the intermolecular forces between the chains. The covalent bonds within the chains are not broken when a polymer melts. Polymers therefore have higher melting points than small molecular substances such as methane or ethanol, but much lower melting points than giant covalent substances such as diamond or silicon dioxide, where strong covalent bonds must be broken.

You need to recognise a polymer from a diagram showing its bonding and structure. Look for a long chain of atoms joined by covalent bonds, often drawn with bonds that continue off the ends of the diagram, or a repeat unit drawn inside brackets with a small n after the bracket. The n stands for a large number of repeat units, so (C₂H₄)n means many C₂H₄ repeat units joined in one chain. Compare this with a small molecule (a few atoms, clearly separate), a giant covalent structure (a continuous three-dimensional network of covalent bonds), an ionic lattice (charged ions) and a metal (positive ions with delocalised electrons).

Like other molecular substances, polymers do not conduct electricity. They have no free electrons or ions that can move and carry charge, which is why plastics are used to insulate electrical wires and make plugs and switches.
keyFacts: Polymers have very large molecules (long chains).
Atoms within a polymer molecule are linked by strong covalent bonds.
The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong because the molecules are so large.
Polymers are solids at room temperature.
Melting a polymer overcomes intermolecular forces between chains; covalent bonds in the chains are not broken.
Polymers melt at higher temperatures than small molecules but lower than giant covalent structures.
A repeat unit in brackets followed by n shows a polymer, for example (C₂H₄)n for poly(ethene).
Polymers do not conduct electricity because they have no free electrons or ions.

keyTerms.definition: A substance made of very large molecules formed from many repeat units joined by covalent bonds into long chains.
The small section of a polymer chain that is repeated many times along the chain.
A strong bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons.
The forces of attraction between separate molecules. They are much weaker than covalent bonds but get stronger as molecules get larger.
A common polymer made from many ethene molecules joined together; its repeat unit has the formula C₂H₄.

workedExamples.title: Counting atoms in a polymer molecule
workedExamples.question: A molecule of poly(ethene) contains 3000 repeat units. Each repeat unit has the formula C₂H₄. Calculate the number of carbon atoms and the number of hydrogen atoms in the molecule.
steps: Each repeat unit contains 2 carbon atoms and 4 hydrogen atoms.

workedExamples.title: Explaining a melting point
workedExamples.question: Methane (CH₄) is a gas at room temperature but poly(ethene) is a solid. Both contain carbon and hydrogen joined by covalent bonds. Explain the difference.
steps: Both are molecular: the covalent bonds inside the molecules are strong and are not broken on melting or boiling.
Changing state overcomes the intermolecular forces between molecules.
Methane molecules are very small, so the intermolecular forces are very weak and little energy is needed to overcome them.
Poly(ethene) molecules are very large, so the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong and much more energy is needed.
workedExamples.answer: Poly(ethene) has much larger molecules, so the intermolecular forces between molecules are stronger and need more energy to overcome; it is therefore a solid at room temperature while methane is a gas.

diagrams.title: Polymer chains and intermolecular forces
diagrams.caption: Each line is one polymer molecule. Dashed lines represent intermolecular forces between neighbouring chains. Because the chains are so long, these forces are relatively strong overall, so the polymer is a solid at room temperature.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that when a polymer melts, the covalent bonds in the chains break.
misconceptions.right: In fact melting only overcomes the intermolecular forces between the chains. The chains stay intact; if the covalent bonds broke, the substance would decompose rather than melt.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think polymers are giant covalent structures like diamond.
misconceptions.right: In fact a polymer is made of separate, very large molecules. There are no covalent bonds between chains, only intermolecular forces, so polymers melt at much lower temperatures than diamond or silicon dioxide.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think intermolecular forces are the bonds holding the atoms together inside a molecule.
misconceptions.right: In fact intermolecular forces act between separate molecules. The bonds inside a polymer molecule are covalent bonds, which are much stronger.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the n in (C₂H₄)n means the polymer contains a small, fixed number of atoms.
misconceptions.right: In fact n represents a large number of repeat units, often thousands, which is why polymer molecules are so large.

realWorld: Poly(ethene) is used for carrier bags, food packaging and bottles because it is a tough, flexible solid at room temperature.
Plastics such as PVC are used to insulate electrical cables because polymers do not conduct electricity.
Plastic kettles and food containers that are heated must be made from polymers with high enough melting points not to soften at the temperatures used.
examTips: When explaining why a polymer is a solid, say 'intermolecular forces between the polymer molecules are relatively strong' and link this to the large size of the molecules. Do not say the covalent bonds are broken.
Always say 'between molecules' for intermolecular forces and 'within molecules' for covalent bonds. Mixing these up loses marks.
To recognise a polymer in a diagram, look for a long chain with bonds continuing off the ends, or brackets with n after them.
If asked to compare melting points, use the order: small molecules lowest, polymers higher, giant covalent structures highest, and explain each using what has to be overcome.
summary: Polymers have very large, chain-like molecules.
Atoms in the chains are joined by strong covalent bonds.
Intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong because the molecules are large.
So polymers are solids at room temperature.
Melting overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds.
A repeat unit in brackets with n identifies a polymer.

questions.question: What type of bond links the atoms within a polymer molecule?
options: Ionic bonds
Strong covalent bonds
Weak intermolecular forces
Metallic bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: Strong covalent bonds
questions.explanation: The atoms in a polymer chain share pairs of electrons, so they are joined by strong covalent bonds. Intermolecular forces act between chains, not within them.

questions.question: What is the state of poly(ethene) at room temperature?
options: Solid
Liquid
Gas
It changes directly from solid to gas at room temperature
markScheme: 1 mark: Solid
questions.explanation: Polymers are solids at room temperature because the intermolecular forces between their very large molecules are relatively strong.

questions.question: Which of these substances is a polymer?
options: Methane
Sodium chloride
Poly(ethene)
Diamond
markScheme: 1 mark: Poly(ethene)
questions.explanation: Poly(ethene) is made of very long chain molecules. Methane is a small molecule, sodium chloride is ionic and diamond is a giant covalent structure.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the molecules in a polymer?
options: They are very small, with only a few atoms each
They are very large, long-chain molecules
They are positive and negative ions
They are atoms all joined in one continuous three-dimensional network
markScheme: 1 mark: They are very large, long-chain molecules
questions.explanation: Polymer molecules are very large chains made from many repeat units. A continuous three-dimensional network describes a giant covalent structure such as diamond, not a polymer.

questions.question: Why are polymers solids at room temperature?
options: The intermolecular forces between the large polymer molecules are relatively strong
There are strong covalent bonds between the polymer molecules
The polymer chains are held together by ionic bonds
Polymers contain delocalised electrons that hold the chains together
markScheme: 1 mark: The intermolecular forces between the large polymer molecules are relatively strong
questions.explanation: Polymer molecules are very large, so the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong. There are no covalent or ionic bonds between separate chains, and polymers have no delocalised electrons.

questions.question: When poly(ethene) is heated until it melts, what is overcome?
options: The covalent bonds between carbon atoms in the chain
The covalent bonds between carbon and hydrogen atoms
Ionic bonds between the chains
The intermolecular forces between the chains
markScheme: 1 mark: The intermolecular forces between the chains
questions.explanation: Melting lets the chains move past each other, which needs the intermolecular forces between the chains to be overcome. The covalent bonds inside the chains stay intact.

questions.question: Four substances are described below. Which one is a polymer?
options: Molecules each made of three atoms joined by covalent bonds
A lattice of positive and negative ions held by strong electrostatic forces
Separate molecules, each a chain of thousands of atoms joined by covalent bonds
Atoms each joined to four others by covalent bonds in a continuous network
markScheme: 1 mark: Separate molecules, each a chain of thousands of atoms joined by covalent bonds
questions.explanation: A polymer consists of separate, very long chain molecules. Three-atom molecules are small molecules, the ion lattice is ionic, and the continuous network is a giant covalent structure.

questions.question: How do the intermolecular forces between poly(ethene) molecules compare with those between methane (CH₄) molecules?
options: Stronger, because poly(ethene) molecules are much larger
Weaker, because poly(ethene) molecules are much larger
The same, because both contain only carbon and hydrogen
Poly(ethene) has no intermolecular forces because its atoms are covalently bonded
markScheme: 1 mark: Stronger, because poly(ethene) molecules are much larger
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules. Poly(ethene) molecules are far larger than methane molecules, so the forces between them are stronger.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the repeating unit of poly(ethene).
The formula of poly(ethene) can be written as (C₂H₄)n.
What does n represent?

options: The number of carbon atoms in one repeat unit
A large number of repeat units joined in one molecule
The number of hydrogen atoms in the whole molecule
The number of separate polymer molecules in a sample
markScheme: 1 mark: A large number of repeat units joined in one molecule
questions.explanation: The bracket contains one repeat unit and n shows that it is repeated a large number of times along a single chain.

questions.question: Which statement correctly explains the melting point of a polymer compared with methane and diamond?
options: It is the highest of the three because polymers contain the most covalent bonds
It is the lowest of the three because polymer chains are tangled
It is higher than diamond because intermolecular forces are stronger than covalent bonds
It is between them: its intermolecular forces are stronger than methane's, but no covalent bonds break, unlike in diamond
markScheme: 1 mark: It is between them: its intermolecular forces are stronger than methane's, but no covalent bonds break, unlike in diamond
questions.explanation: Polymers have stronger intermolecular forces than small molecules, so they melt at a higher temperature than methane. Melting diamond requires breaking strong covalent bonds, which needs far more energy.

questions.question: A student says: 'Polymers have high melting points because covalent bonds are strong.' What is wrong with this statement?
options: Covalent bonds are actually weak
The covalent bonds in the chains are not broken when a polymer melts; only intermolecular forces are overcome
Polymers do not contain covalent bonds
Polymers are held together by ionic bonds, not covalent bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: The covalent bonds in the chains are not broken when a polymer melts; only intermolecular forces are overcome
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are strong, but they are not what is overcome when a polymer melts. Melting overcomes the intermolecular forces between chains.

questions.question: State what is meant by a polymer.
markScheme: 1 mark: a substance with very large (long-chain) molecules made of many repeat units joined together
questions.explanation: The key idea is that polymer molecules are very large, made from many repeat units linked by covalent bonds.

questions.question: Name the type of force that acts between separate polymer molecules.
markScheme: 1 mark: intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Covalent bonds are within molecules; the forces acting between separate molecules are intermolecular forces.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the formulae of four substances.
Give the formula of the substance that is a polymer.
markScheme: 1 mark: (C₂H₄)n
questions.explanation: The bracket with n shows a repeat unit repeated many times, which identifies a polymer. H₂O and CH₄ are small molecules and NaCl is ionic.

questions.question: Describe the structure and bonding in a polymer.
acceptedAnswers: very large molecules or long chains
atoms joined by strong covalent bonds
markScheme: 1 mark: very large molecules / long chains of atoms
1 mark: atoms within each chain linked by (strong) covalent bonds, with intermolecular forces between chains
questions.explanation: A full answer covers both levels: covalent bonds inside the chains and intermolecular forces between the separate chains.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of water and a polymer.
Explain, in terms of the size of the molecules, why the polymer has the higher melting point.
acceptedAnswers: more energy needed to overcome intermolecular forces
markScheme: 1 mark: polymer molecules are much larger than water molecules
1 mark: so the intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them
questions.explanation: Intermolecular forces increase with molecule size. Both melt by overcoming intermolecular forces, but the forces between large polymer chains are stronger.

questions.question: A student says: 'When a polymer melts, the polymer chains break into smaller pieces.' Explain why the student is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: chains stay intact and move past each other
markScheme: 1 mark: melting only overcomes the intermolecular forces between the chains
1 mark: the strong covalent bonds within the chains are not broken, so the chains stay the same length
questions.explanation: During melting the chains gain enough energy to slide past one another. Breaking the covalent bonds would change the substance, which is not what melting is.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of three substances.
Explain why the polymer has a higher melting point than methane but a much lower melting point than silicon dioxide.
acceptedAnswers: covalent bonds broken to melt silicon dioxide
covalent bonds much stronger than intermolecular forces
markScheme: 1 mark: polymer molecules are larger than methane molecules so the intermolecular forces are stronger
1 mark: silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure, so melting it requires breaking (many) strong covalent bonds
1 mark: covalent bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces, so far more energy is needed
questions.explanation: The answer must name what is overcome in each case: intermolecular forces for methane and the polymer, covalent bonds for silicon dioxide.

questions.question: Suggest why polymers are used to cover electrical wires.
markScheme: 1 mark: polymers do not conduct electricity (they are insulators) because they have no free electrons or ions
questions.explanation: Molecular substances, including polymers, have no charged particles that are free to move, so they are good electrical insulators.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a section of a poly(ethene) chain containing 6 carbon atoms.
The hydrogen atoms are not shown.
Each carbon atom is bonded to 2 hydrogen atoms.
Calculate the number of hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbon atoms in this section.

questions.question:
A poly(ethene) molecule contains 2000 repeat units.
Each repeat unit has the formula C₂H₄.
Calculate the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.
questions.explanation: Each repeat unit has 2 carbon atoms, so 2000 repeat units contain 2000 × 2 = 4000 carbon atoms.

questions.question:
A poly(ethene) molecule contains 15 000 repeat units.
Each repeat unit has the formula C₂H₄.
Calculate the total number of atoms in the molecule.
markScheme: 1 mark: each repeat unit contains 6 atoms (2 C + 4 H)
questions.explanation: One C₂H₄ unit has 2 + 4 = 6 atoms. 15 000 × 6 = 90 000 atoms. A common mistake is to count only the carbon atoms (30 000).

questions.question:
The repeat unit of poly(ethene) is C₂H₄.
A poly(ethene) molecule has 5000 repeat units.
Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of the molecule.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12 H = 1
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr of repeat unit = (2 × 12) + (4 × 1) = 28
questions.explanation: First find the mass of one repeat unit (28), then multiply by the number of repeat units. This large value shows how big polymer molecules are.

questions.question:
A sample of poly(ethene) has molecules with a relative formula mass (Mr) of 56 000.
The repeat unit of poly(ethene) is C₂H₄.
Calculate the number of repeat units in each molecule.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12 H = 1
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr of C₂H₄ = 28
questions.explanation: Divide the Mr of the whole molecule by the Mr of one repeat unit: 56 000 ÷ 28 = 2000.

markScheme: Indicative content: poly(ethene) is a polymer; it is made of very large molecules (long chains); many repeat units (C₂H₄) joined; atoms within each chain are joined by strong covalent bonds (shared pairs of electrons); the chains are separate molecules; intermolecular forces act between the chains; these forces are relatively strong because the molecules are so large; a lot of energy is needed to overcome them; so poly(ethene) is a solid at room temperature; covalent bonds are not broken on melting.

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the structure and bonding at both levels (covalent bonds within chains, intermolecular forces between chains) linked to the size of the molecules to explain the solid state.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant points, for example long chains or covalent bonds, but the explanation of why it is a solid is missing or confused (for example, says covalent bonds are broken).
questions.explanation: The best answers describe the long chains, the covalent bonds within them and the relatively strong intermolecular forces between them, and use the size of the molecules to explain why it is solid.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the melting points of three substances.
Explain the differences in the melting points of these substances in terms of their structure and bonding.
markScheme: Indicative content: methane is made of small molecules; atoms joined by covalent bonds within each molecule; weak intermolecular forces between molecules; little energy needed to overcome them, so very low melting point. Poly(ethene) is a polymer with very large molecules; covalent bonds within chains; intermolecular forces between chains are relatively strong because the molecules are large; more energy needed to overcome them so higher melting point than methane; covalent bonds in chains are not broken on melting. Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure; every atom joined to others by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network; no separate molecules; melting requires breaking many strong covalent bonds; very large amount of energy needed so very high melting point. Covalent bonds are much stronger than intermolecular forces.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and coherent explanation of all three substances, correctly identifying what is overcome in each case (intermolecular forces or covalent bonds) and linking this to the relative amounts of energy needed.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains at least two substances correctly, or all three with some confusion between covalent bonds and intermolecular forces.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about structure or bonding, for example 'silicon dioxide has strong bonds', with little link to melting point.
questions.explanation: The key to top marks is saying exactly what is overcome on melting: weak intermolecular forces (methane), stronger intermolecular forces between large molecules (poly(ethene)) and strong covalent bonds (silicon dioxide).

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two ways of representing poly(ethene).
The section of chain has bonds continuing off both ends.
The repeat unit is drawn in brackets with a small n beside it.

markScheme: 1 mark: the bonds continuing off the ends show the chain continues (it is only part of a very long molecule)
1 mark: the box is a repeat unit and n shows it is repeated a large number of times
questions.explanation: Both features tell you the molecule is very large and made of many repeating units, which is what defines a polymer.
